260.title: One dark night
260.hook: his poem: a soul slips out of the sleeping house to meet her beloved
260.carry: my house being now at rest
260.howItsDone: Catholics read John's poem The Dark Night and his commentaries on it, often with a spiritual director, to understand seasons when prayer and faith feel dark, and Carmelites pray and sing his poems.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the escape: a rope of blankets, a fall, and nuns who hid him. Your line was out the window. Today, the poem that came out of all that darkness.

Someone's going through a dark night of the soul. People use the phrase for burnout, a breakup, a bad year, a crisis of faith. It's on book covers and in song lyrics. It goes back to a poem of eight short stanzas by a small, thin friar, written, tradition says, close to the months when he climbed out of a prison window. And here's the surprise: it isn't a sad poem. It's a love poem.
screen: `A DARK NIGHT OF THE SOUL.` → `FROM EIGHT SHORT STANZAS.` → `NOT A SAD POEM. A LOVE POEM.`

segments.voice: First, the story. The poem begins, in John's Spanish: "En una noche oscura," on a dark night. A young woman, burning with love, slips out of her house while everyone sleeps. The first stanza ends "estando ya mi casa sosegada," my house being now at rest. Nobody sees her. She takes a secret stair, in disguise. She carries no light except the one burning in her heart, and it guides her more surely than the noonday sun, to where her beloved is waiting. Second, who's who. For John, the young woman is the soul, and the beloved is God. The sleeping house is everything in us that usually runs the show: our appetites, our worries, our need to control. When the house finally goes quiet, the soul can slip out to meet God. Third, the turn. Oh night that guided me, she sings, oh night more lovely than the dawn. The darkness isn't the enemy. Without it, she'd never have slipped out unseen. Fourth, the books. John knew his poem needed explaining, so he wrote two whole books about it, the Ascent of Mount Carmel and the Dark Night. In them, the night describes how God leads a soul through times when the old lights go out. Over the next days, i'll walk through those books with you. But start here, with the poem: a night that's also a love story.
screen: `SHE SLIPS OUT, UNSEEN.` · `THE SOUL, GOD, THE SLEEPING HOUSE.` · `OH NIGHT THAT GUIDED ME.` · `TWO BOOKS TO EXPLAIN ONE POEM.` · then, large: `ESTANDO YA MI CASA SOSEGADA.`

segments.voice: Sit in the dark: turn off the light if you can, or close your eyes and cover them with your hands, and let the house of you go quiet, the lists, the plans, the noise. Don't look for anything; just notice that the dark isn't empty. If you pray, wait for God there, the way the young woman went out to meet her beloved; if you don't, let the dark be a place to rest.
Dark night. From John of the Cross's poem: the night in which the soul, its house at rest, slips out to meet God. Not despair, but a love story. Today's word.
Your line: my house being now at rest. In the dark, she found the way out. See you tomorrow.

261.title: The night of the senses
261.hook: when prayer stops feeling good, God may be weaning us from the sweets
261.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors often turn to John's Dark Night, book one, when people say prayer has gone dry, and encourage them to keep praying faithfully rather than chasing feelings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dark night: a love poem, a sleeping house, a soul slipping out to meet God. Your line was my house being now at rest. Today, John explains the first part of that night.

People who pray don't always say this out loud. At the start, it can feel wonderful. Mass, a quiet church, a psalm read slowly, and something warm comes. Tears, sometimes. Peace. Going back is easy. Then one day it's just gone. Show up, say the words. Nothing. Flat as cardboard. It's easy to conclude that something went wrong, or that God has left, or that it was never real. John of the Cross had a very different explanation.
screen: `AT FIRST, IT FEELS WONDERFUL.` → `THEN ONE DAY, NOTHING.` → `DID GOD LEAVE?`

segments.voice: First, the mother. John opens his book the Dark Night with a homely picture. A loving mother holds her baby close, warms it, and feeds it sweet milk. That's how God treats beginners in prayer, he says: with comfort and sweetness. Second, the weaning. But a mother who loves her child doesn't nurse it forever. One day she weans it. She sets it down so it will learn to walk, and it cries for the milk. Saint Paul says something similar to one young church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not able as yet." John says God does the same with souls. The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so they can grow. Third, the sweet tooth. John is funny and sharp about beginners. He lists their faults in prayer: wanting more and more good feelings, a spiritual sweet tooth; judging others who seem less devout; sulking when prayer is dull. The night of the senses is God's cure for all that. When the feelings dry up, you find out whether you were seeking God, or the sweets God gave. Fourth, dry is not gone. Dryness in prayer, John says, can be a sign that God is closer, not farther, doing the work quietly, below what you can feel. He doesn't say every dry spell is this; tomorrow he gives ways to tell. But he says: don't assume God left because the sweetness did.

segments.voice: Pray even if it's dry: sit, breathe, and don't try to make anything happen. If you pray, just be with God, even if it feels like talking to a wall; that counts. If you don't, sit with something you've been faithful to that doesn't feel exciting anymore, a friendship, a job, a promise, and notice that showing up still matters.

262.title: Three signs (Dark Night 1.9)
262.hook: no taste for things, no ease in meditation, yet a quiet wish for God
262.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors use John's three signs (Dark Night 1.9) to help people discern dryness in prayer, and often also ask about sleep, health and mood, recommending medical or counseling help when needed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sweetness, and how God weans a soul from the sweets. Your line was dry is not gone. Today, how John says to tell.

A dry patch in prayer can come from a lot of places. Maybe you've drifted, and stopped caring. Maybe you're exhausted, or sick, or haven't slept in weeks. Maybe it's something heavier, a depression that makes everything gray, not just prayer. Or maybe it's what John of the Cross called the night of the senses, God quietly at work. From the inside, they can all feel the same. So John, a careful teacher and a good spiritual director, gave three signs to tell them apart.
screen: `DRIFTING? TIRED? DEPRESSED?` → `OR GOD AT WORK?` → `FROM THE INSIDE, THE SAME.`

segments.voice: They're in the Dark Night, book one, chapter nine. First sign: no taste for anything. Prayer has lost its sweetness, but so has everything else you might run to instead. You haven't swapped God for something shinier. Nothing much satisfies. John says that matters: if you'd simply drifted, you'd be enjoying something else. Second sign: the quiet wish. This is the key. Even in the dryness, your mind keeps turning to God, with a painful kind of care. You worry that you're not serving God, that you're going backward. John says that very worry is a good sign. Someone who had truly stopped caring wouldn't worry at all. The longing stays, even when the feelings go. Third sign: meditation won't work anymore. The old way of praying, thinking through a Gospel scene, picturing it, working at it, won't go. Your mind slides off. John says God is beginning to give himself in a quieter, simpler way, beneath thinking. So don't strain at the old methods. Rest, quietly and lovingly. Fourth, an honest caution. John himself says dryness can also come from what he calls melancholy, from the body, and that it's different: the quiet longing for God is missing. Today we'd say plainly: if a heaviness sits on everything, sleep, food, work, joy, not just prayer, talk to a doctor or a counselor. Many Catholic spiritual directors say the same. Grace and good care aren't rivals.
screen: `ONE: NO TASTE FOR ANYTHING.` · `TWO: THE QUIET WISH FOR GOD.` · `THREE: MEDITATION WON'T GO.` · `A CAUTION: CARE FOR THE BODY TOO.` · then, large: `THE LONGING STAYS.`

segments.voice: Without judging yourself, ask gently what prayer is like for you right now: sweet, flat, or somewhere between; whether other things feel flat too; whether a quiet wish is still underneath, for God or for something good. There are no wrong answers: if you pray, tell God what you find, and if you don't, just notice. And if something heavy is there, let this be the moment you decide to tell someone.
Three signs. John's way to recognize the night of the senses: no taste for anything, a quiet, anxious wish for God, and meditation that won't go. Today's word.

263.title: The night of the spirit
263.hook: a deeper night, where even our ideas of God are purified
263.howItsDone: Catholics who experience long seasons of spiritual darkness are often pointed to the second book of John's Dark Night, usually with an experienced spiritual director, and the Church remembers saints such as Thérèse of Lisieux who described similar nights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three signs to tell the night of the senses from drifting or illness. Your line was the longing stays. Today, John says there's a second, deeper night.

A kind old man on a cloud. A stern one. A very large grandfather, or a referee with a whistle. Those are pictures of God a child might draw, and a child can outgrow them. But John of the Cross says grown-ups carry pictures of God too: God as my cheerleader, God as a rule book, God as the one who'll make my life work out. And he says there's a night in which even those get taken away.
screen: `A MAN ON A CLOUD.` → `GROWN-UP PICTURES OF GOD.` → `A NIGHT THAT TAKES THEM AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, who it's for. John says the night of the senses is common, and the night of the spirit is for fewer people, those who have already come a long way in prayer. It goes deeper. The first night weaned us from sweet feelings. This one reaches our understanding, our memory and our will, the very ways we think about God. Second, the ray of darkness. Look straight at the sun and you see nothing. You're blinded, not by too little light, but by too much. So when God's light strikes a soul that isn't ready for it, John says, it feels like darkness. He borrows a phrase from an older Christian writer, Dionysius: a ray of darkness. Third, the pain. John doesn't soften this. People in this night can feel abandoned, dry, even rejected by God, like the writer of Lamentations sitting in the ruins. Their old ideas of God don't hold up anymore, and nothing has taken their place yet. It's frightening. John says it's also love: God is making room for himself, the real God, not our picture. Fourth, bigger than your idea. The prophet Isaiah hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor your ways my ways, saith the Lord." Any idea of God we can hold in our heads, John says, is smaller than God. That doesn't make the ideas useless; the Church's teaching still stands. But the God it points to is always larger. Losing a picture, for John, isn't losing God. It can be finding him.

segments.voice: Notice one picture of God you carry: the referee, the distant boss, the one who's disappointed in you, the one who owes you a good life. Just see it, then gently set it down, without rushing to replace it. If you pray, simply say, you're more than this; if you don't, hold the idea that whatever is deepest is larger than your picture of it.

264.title: Nada (Ascent of Mount Carmel)
264.hook: his drawing of the mountain: nothing, nothing, nothing, and on the mountain, nothing
264.howItsDone: Carmelites and many Catholics study John's sketch of Mount Carmel and the nada verses from the Ascent, often as a guide to detachment in Lent or on retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah, where even our ideas of God are purified. Your line was bigger than your idea. Today, one small Spanish word, drawn on a mountain.

A friar sits down and draws a mountain for a convent of nuns. Paths wind up it, with words written along them. It's John, after his escape. He's been sent south, and in the town of Beas he visits the Carmelite nuns as their confessor and teacher. So he does something teachers still do: he draws a diagram. He makes copies and hands them out, so each nun can keep one in her breviary. And written again and again up the middle path is today's word.
screen: `A FRIAR DRAWS A MOUNTAIN.` → `FOR THE NUNS OF BEAS.` → `A COPY FOR EACH BREVIARY.`

segments.voice: First, the two wide roads. On the left and right of John's mountain are broad paths. One is labeled with the goods of earth: possessions, pleasure, knowledge, comfort. The other with the goods of heaven: glory, joy, consolation, even spiritual rewards. Both look sensible. Both wind around and stop short of the top. Second, the narrow way. Straight up the middle runs a thin path, and on it John writes one Spanish word, over and over: nada, nada, nada, nada. Nothing. And near the top: and even on the mountain, nothing. Third, the verses. Beside the drawing, and later in his book the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John writes lines that turn on this word. In his Spanish: "Para venir a gustarlo todo, no quieras tener gusto en nada." To come to enjoy everything, desire to have enjoyment in nothing. To come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing. To come to be everything, desire to be nothing. Fourth, what it means. It sounds bleak. It isn't meant to be. John isn't saying the world is bad, or that people don't matter. His point is about grasping. Cling to anything, even good things, even spiritual things, and your hands are full. Nada is emptying the hands. And the promise at the top of the drawing isn't nothing. It's everything, which is God. Nothing, then everything: the order is the lesson.

segments.voice: Open your hands on your knees, palms up, and think of one thing you've been wanting hard: a purchase, a result, someone's approval, even a certain feeling in prayer. Picture it resting in your open hands, and stop gripping; you don't have to throw it away. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, notice how open hands feel.

265.title: The bird on a thread (Ascent 1.11)
265.hook: a bird tied by a thin thread can't fly any more than one tied by a cord
265.howItsDone: Catholics often use John's bird-on-a-thread image in examinations of conscience and Lenten practices, looking for small voluntary attachments rather than only for large sins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nada: nothing, nothing, nothing up the narrow path. Your line was nothing, then everything. Today, one of John's simplest pictures.

Things hardly worth mentioning. The phone, checked again and again. The grudge against one cousin. The need to be right in the group chat. The show that has to be finished tonight. A little pride in looking busy. Nobody would call any of it an addiction. Small stuff. Harmless. Thin little threads, really. John of the Cross has a picture for exactly those small things, and it isn't as gentle as it sounds.
screen: `THINGS HARDLY WORTH MENTIONING.` → `THE PHONE, THE GRUDGE, THE PRIDE.` → `THIN LITTLE THREADS.`

segments.voice: First, the bird. In the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John says it makes little difference whether a bird is tied by a thin thread or a thick cord. Either way, it can't fly. Sure, the thread is easier to break. But until it's broken, the bird is held just as firmly as if it were tied with rope. Second, what counts as a thread. John is specific, and surprisingly ordinary: being attached to a person, a piece of clothing, a book, a room, a certain kind of food, a bit of gossip, a small pleasure in knowing things. None of these are sins in themselves. What matters is the voluntary clinging, the grip we choose and keep choosing. He's not talking about the natural wants everyone has, which come and go on their own. He means the ones we hold on to. Third, the little fish. He borrows an old belief about a tiny fish, the remora, said to fasten itself to a great ship and slow it down. Small thing, big ship. The size of the attachment isn't the point. The holding is. Fourth, why he cares. John doesn't want us miserable. He says it's a pitiful thing to see people who have given up great things stay held by something small. A favorite cup. A grudge. So close to flying. Just one thread. And the image carries its own hope: a thread is far easier to break than a cord.

266.title: Faith as a dark light (Ascent 2)
266.hook: faith guides like a light we can't look at directly
266.howItsDone: Catholics describe faith as trust in what God has revealed rather than in what they can see or prove, and spiritual directors in the Carmelite tradition steer people away from seeking visions toward plain faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, remora: a thin thread holds as well as a cord. Your line was a thread still holds. Today, how John says we find our way in the dark.

Driving a country road at night, you never see your own headlights. You see by them: the white line, the edge of the ditch, a deer by the fence, a few yards of road at a time. Beyond that, black. You couldn't describe the light itself, and yet everything you see out there comes through it. John of the Cross says faith works something like that. It's a light. But from the inside, it feels like darkness.
screen: `A COUNTRY ROAD AT NIGHT.` → `YOU SEE BY THE HEADLIGHTS.` → `A LIGHT THAT FEELS LIKE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, a dark night. In the second book of the Ascent, John calls faith itself a dark night for the soul. Faith asks us to trust what we can't see, touch or prove, on the word of God. That's dark to the mind, which wants to see for itself. But, he adds, the darker it is for the mind, the more light it gives the soul. Second, the cloud. John points to the Exodus story. As Israel escapes Egypt, a pillar of cloud stands between them and the army chasing them. The Douay-Rheims says: "it was a dark cloud, and enlightening the night." Dark on one side, light on the other. The same cloud. That's faith, John says: darkness to our understanding, light for our way. Third, the walk. Saint Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we walk by faith, and not by sight." Walking isn't understanding. You can walk a path whose end you can't see, one step, in trust. Fourth, why not visions? John warns against chasing visions, voices and special signs. They can mislead, he says, and even true ones can become something to cling to. Faith is the surer guide, precisely because it's plain, humble and dark. Now look back at the week. One dark night, and a house at rest. Sweetness: dry is not gone. Three signs: the longing stays. Isaiah: bigger than your idea. Nada: nothing, then everything. A bird on a thread. And today, a light we can't look at but see by. It's all one night.

segments.voice: Think of something unresolved in your life, where you can't see the end: a diagnosis, a job, a child's choices, a question about God. If you pray, hand the unseen part to God and ask only for the next step; if you don't, name the one step you can see.
